name: Aker Stadion
label: Aker Stadion
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/74887533: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Aker Stadion' (195 m across).
notes: Home ground of Molde FK, seen across the harbour.

text.description: Aker Stadion is the home ground of Molde football club, and it sits right on the edge of the Moldefjord at Reknes, just west of the town centre. It is a big, clean-lined building. The outside is clad in two colours of granite, with glass and aluminium, so it gives a strong shape against the water and sky. It was designed by the architect Kjell Kosberg and opened on 18 April 1998. A year later it won the City Prize, a Norwegian award for building projects that improve the surrounding area. Locals sometimes call it "Røkkeløkka", after the businessman who paid for most of it. It holds a little over 11,000 spectators, so the structure is large but not overwhelming, and it fits into a phone frame well from a short distance away. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m east of the subject. That distance is useful because you can fit the whole building in one shot without tilting the phone upwards. Look for the long granite and glass walls, the roofline and any clear sky above. If the fjord is visible beside the stadium, include a slice of water to give the picture a sense of place.
text.geographic_location: Aker Stadion is at Reknes, on the shore of the Moldefjord, just west of Molde town centre.
text.directions_text: Start from Molde town centre and head west towards Reknes on the fjord shore; the stadium is the large building by the water. There is no public transport stop listed for this spot, but the stadium can be reached on foot from the town centre. The phone icon on the map is about 230 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x), which fits the whole stadium from this distance. Try telephoto (2x or more) for a tighter shot of the facade and roofline.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 230 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west. From here the stadium sits in the middle of the view with room around it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and place the stadium on one of the lower thirds, with sky above. Keep the phone level so the long horizontal lines of the building stay straight. If you can see the fjord, include a strip of water at the edge of the frame. For a tighter second picture, zoom in on the granite and glass of the facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the stadium to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the building keeps its colour. Check that the picture is straight before you take it.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a dry day with some light on the front of the stadium. Evening light can look warm, but check which way the building faces the sun before you commit to one spot.

text.access_note: The stadium can be photographed from outside in the open; for matches, tours or going inside, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: From the stand-here point, which is east of the stadium, you look west towards the stadium.
Late-day sun in the west may light the stadium from behind when viewed from the east, so the front may be in shade.

name: Varden viewpoint
label: Varden viewpoint
camera_source: Stand-here point set at the correction gate (own photo GPS 2026-11-17).
pin_note: Position from OSM N441387663 (Varden): kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Hilltop lookout over Molde and the fjord with the Romsdal Alps panorama.

text.description:
Varden is a viewpoint in Molde, and the third stop on this map. It is a place to slow down and take in the view rather than a single building or monument to point at. That suits a phone well. A wide scene with layers of land, water and sky is easy to capture, and there is usually time to try a few versions.

The phone icon on the map is about 65 m east of the subject. From there you look west towards it. Stand with the marker in front of you and keep some of the surroundings in the frame, so the picture shows where you are and not only the spot itself.

Start with the default lens (1x) and turn on the gridlines so the horizon stays level. Then switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for a broader view, and try a zoom (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out a single detail in the distance. Tap the screen on the part of the scene you care about most, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky looks too bright. Take a few frames, as the view and the light can change within minutes. Clean the lens with a soft cloth first, because a smudge shows up as haze in wide views.
text.geographic_location: Varden is a viewpoint in Molde.
text.directions_text: No station or tram stop is listed for this spot, so check a local map or transport planner for the route. The phone icon on the map is about 65 m east of the subject. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Use ultra-wide (0.5x) for the full scene and a 2x-5x zoom, depending on your phone, for distant details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand about 65 m east of the subject, at the phone icon on the map, and face west.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on the gridlines and put the horizon on the upper or lower line, depending on whether the land or the sky matters more. Keep a little foreground at the edge of the frame to give a sense of depth.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap to focus on the middle distance and lower the exposure slider a touch if the sky is bright. Try panorama for a sweeping view, moving slowly and keeping the phone level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft light early or late in the day usually flatters a wide view, and a clear day shows the most distance.

text.access_note: Access rules for this viewpoint are not confirmed here, so check the official site before you go.

name: Molde Cathedral
label: Molde Cathedral
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Molde rådhus' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Molde rådhus' (way/231352909): middle (86 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/310662273: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Molde Cathedral' (80 m across).
notes: Main church of Molde, with a tall tower and a modernist design.

text.description:
Molde Cathedral is the town's main church and the seat of the Bishop of Møre. It is a long, white brick building, with a tall bell tower standing free beside it rather than attached. The tower is about 60 metres tall. The present church was designed by the architect Finn Bryn and consecrated on 8 December 1957. It is the third church on this site. The one before it burned down when Molde was bombed on 29 April 1940. It became a cathedral in 1983, when the Diocese of Møre was created.

The best photo is taken from above. The small roof park of the town hall (Molde rådhus) faces the cathedral across the square. From there you see the white walls and the separate tower, with the fjord and the mountains behind the town. It is also a small rose garden, and a 2026 guide calls it the best place for a picture with the roses in the foreground. Stand at the edge of the roof park, let a few roses fill the bottom of the frame, and keep the tower upright and central. The roof park is described as free to enter during business hours, but check the official site before you go. If you also want a close-up of the entrance or the tower base, you can walk down to the square afterwards.
text.geographic_location: The cathedral stands in the centre of Molde, in the town-centre area next to the square that the town hall faces.
text.directions_text: Start from Molde town centre. The town hall is on the square facing the cathedral, so head for the town hall and its roof park, the recommended viewpoint nearby. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to take in the whole cathedral, the tower and some of the fjord behind. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want a lot of roses in the foreground. Use 2x or 3x telephoto, if your phone has it, to pick out the tower and the white brick walls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Molde rådhus (roof park of the town hall, facing the cathedral across the square). The cathedral's white brick body and free-standing bell tower seen from above, with the fjord and surrounding mountains behind the town. The town hall roof park (Molde rådhus) is the recommended viewpoint nearby. From this side you look across towards the cathedral, with its white brick body and free-standing bell tower, and the fjord and mountains behind the town.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the tower on one of the vertical lines, with the church body along the lower third. Keep a few roses at the bottom edge for depth, and hold the phone level so the tower does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the white wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the brick keeps its detail and does not turn bright white. For the roses, tap on a flower and check that the cathedral behind still looks sharp enough.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Bright, even daylight suits the white brick, but any clear day with the mountains visible behind the town works well.

text.access_note: The cathedral is a working place of worship and the town hall roof park is described as free during business hours, so check the official sites before you go for opening times and any visiting rules.

name: Teatret Vårt
label: Teatret Vårt
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Gørvellplassen' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Gørvellplassen' (way/43542382): middle (115 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/9866508417: the OpenStreetMap point 'Teatret Vårt'.
notes: The town's regional theatre in the centre.

text.description:
Teatret Vårt is the regional theatre for Møre og Romsdal county. It was established in 1972 and is based in Molde. It also works with the annual Molde International Jazz Festival. The theatre is housed in the Plassen building, a large granite structure that fills the city square. Its architect describes it as literally gripping the square, and that is what makes it a good subject for a phone photo. The stone mass, the broad staircase and the stepped seating rising towards the roof give you strong shapes and lines, even on a quiet day.

The best view is from the square itself, Gørvellplassen, where you can see the building's full form from the front. If you want something different, walk to the foot of the building, at Plassen. From there you can photograph the wide stone staircase and the facade, with the seating stepping up towards the roof.

Keep your phone level so the long edges of the building stay straight. Use the gridlines to help, and leave a little space around the building so it sits in the square rather than filling the whole frame. Add a person on the steps or in the square if you want to show the scale.
text.geographic_location: Teatret Vårt is in the centre of Molde, in the Plassen building on the city square, Gørvellplassen.
text.directions_text: No tram or train stops are listed for this spot, so start from Molde town centre and head for the city square, Gørvellplassen. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole granite building and some of the square into one frame. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural view of the facade. A telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) is useful for details of the stonework and the stepped seating.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Gørvellplassen. The granite Plassen building filling the city square, which is the main frontal view of the theatre's home. From here the Plassen building fills the square in front of you and you see the main frontal view of the theatre's home, with the theatre just to the north.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the building's horizontal edges with them. Keep the phone level and at chest height to avoid leaning verticals. Include a bit of the square in the foreground to show how the building grips it. As an alternative, go to the foot of the building at Plassen and photograph the broad stone staircase and facade, with the stepped seating rising towards the roof.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the facade to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the pale stone or sky looks washed out. Check the edges of the ultra-wide shot, as buildings can stretch near the corners.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft daylight usually suits the stone best. At dusk, try night mode with your phone resting against something steady.

text.access_note: The square is an open public space, but check the official site before you go if you want to use the staircase, go inside or go up to the roof.

name: Kongebjørka
label: Kongebjørka
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Fredslunden' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Fredslunden' (way/169850116): middle (33 m across).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/1810092584: the OpenStreetMap point 'Kongebjørka'.
notes: Birch tree where King Haakon VII and the royal family rested in 1940.

text.description:
Kongebjørka, the Royal Birch, is a Norwegian national symbol and a memorial to the Nazi occupation of Norway. It stands at Glomstua in Molde. In the last weekend of April 1940, King Haakon VII and Crown Prince Olav sheltered under a birch here during a German bombing raid, and Per Bratland photographed them. The picture travelled around the world, and it also inspired the poet Nordahl Grieg to write his poem Kongen.

The tree you see today is not the original. The first birch was vandalised in 1981, its replacement was destroyed in the 1992 New Year storm, and King Harald V planted a third tree afterwards. A memorial was put up nearby in 1955, and the Peace Grove (Fredslunden) was inaugurated in 1997.

The site photographs well because you can tell two stories from one spot. Close to the birch, you get the tree with the stone relief of the 1940 photograph, which is the classic view. The birch and its memorial sit among trees planted by notable visitors. Benches in the grove make it easy to pause and compose the shot without rushing. Take both: one close frame of the relief and one wide frame of the whole grove.
text.geographic_location: Kongebjørka is at Glomstua in Molde, in Møre og Romsdal.
text.directions_text: No Underground, tram or train stops are listed for this spot. Glomstua is in Molde, so check a map app on your phone for the route. The birch is just to the north of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Use the default lens (1x) for the grove as a whole. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the trees and benches do not fit. Use telephoto (2x or more, depending on your phone) for the stone relief on the birch.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Fredslunden (the grove next to the birch). A quieter wider view that places the birch and its memorial inside the Peace Grove, with trees planted by notable visitors. The birch and its memorial lie just to the north of you, set inside the Peace Grove. For the classic close view of the tree with the relief of the 1940 photograph, walk up to Kongebjørka itself.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: From the grove, include some of the surrounding trees so the birch is clearly part of a larger place. Turn on gridlines and place the birch on one of the vertical lines rather than dead centre. Keep the horizon level. Then step closer for a tighter shot of the relief, holding your phone straight on so the stone does not lean.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the birch to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly if the sky is bright, so the leaves and stone keep their detail. Portrait mode is not needed here, as the whole scene looks best sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Choose a time of day when the light is soft, such as morning or an overcast day, so the stone relief has no harsh shadows. Birch leaves look freshest in summer.

text.access_note: This is an outdoor memorial and park, but opening arrangements are unclear, so check locally or on the official site before you go.

Then take a few steps closer and try a tighter version with the telephoto lens (2x or more, depending on your phone) to pick out detail and keep the background simple. Turn on the gridlines in your camera settings to keep the horizon and any vertical lines straight. If people walk through the frame, wait a moment or take a Live Photo and choose the best frame afterwards. Wipe your lens with a clean cloth first, as a smudge is the most common reason for a hazy picture.

name: Romsdal Museum
label: Romsdal Museum
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bygata' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bygata på Romsdalsmuseet' (node/6612575940): point.
pin_note: Position from Wikidata Q6516023: kept: no OpenStreetMap object carries this Wikidata ID.
notes: Open-air museum of old wooden buildings by the fjord.

text.description:
The Romsdal Museum is an open-air folk museum on the old Reknes farm in Molde. It was founded in 1912 by Peter Tønder Solemdal and opened to the public in 1928. It is counted among the largest and most extensive folk museums in Norway. The open-air collection has more than 40 buildings from the Romsdal region, dating from the 16th to the 20th centuries. The grounds also hold a small lake popular with local birds, the old ice pond (Isdammen) and the stage used during the Moldejazz festival.

The best picture is on Bygata, the reconstructed town street. It shows what much of Molde looked like before the 1916 fire and the 1940 bombing. A row of restored town houses lines the street, and the modern timber Krona building is visible at the far end. The old and new buildings together make a good photo, and the street gives you leading lines and a clear sense of depth.

Stand at the western entrance of the street and shoot along it. Keep the houses straight at the edges, and use gridlines to help. Pick a moment when few people are in the street, so the houses stay the subject. If you also want a second view, the modern Krona building makes a good contrast with the old houses. The grounds stay open when the buildings are shut, but the historic houses are closed outside the summer season.
text.geographic_location: The museum grounds are on the former Reknes farm in Molde, in Møre og Romsdal county. The Krona building is visible at the far end of the reconstructed town street.
text.directions_text: No public transport stop is listed for this spot, so check local options for reaching the Romsdal Museum grounds from Molde town centre. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to show the whole street of houses with Krona at the end. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street feels cramped, but keep the phone level so the houses do not lean. Try telephoto (2x or more) to pick out Krona and the nearest house fronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Bygata (the reconstructed town street, viewed from its western entrance by the Krona end). A row of restored pre-war Molde town houses lining the reconstructed street, with the Krona building visible at the far end. The reconstructed town street, and look along the street; Krona is visible at the far end. You see a row of restored pre-war Molde town houses lining the street.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the street up so it leads towards Krona. Keep the rooflines level, and include a little sky and some foreground path or street surface for depth. For a second picture, turn to Krona alone: the new timber building contrasts with the old town houses.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the house fronts to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the timber walls keep their colour. Use portrait mode only for a person standing in the street, not for the buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Soft morning or late-afternoon light suits the house fronts, and early or quiet hours leave the street emptier. Avoid Moldejazz week (week 29), when the park is used for concerts and views may be blocked.

text.access_note: The park grounds stay open when the buildings are closed, but the historic houses are closed outside the summer season, so check the official site before you go.
